title: Fifty Famous Stories Retold
author: James Baldwin
licenseEvidence: Project Gutenberg #18442: 'Public domain in the USA'; first published by the American Book Company in 1896
description: James Baldwin's classic collection of short hero tales and legends, from King Alfred's burned cakes to Horatius at the bridge and Whittington's cat. Each day you read one or two stories aloud, your child tells it back, and then draws a favorite scene. A gentle first taste of history for ages 7 to 10, and the full text is free online.
includes: 34 lessons in 7 units covering all 50 stories
Link to the free full text for every story
A narration prompt and a drawing prompt for each lesson
One question per story, with answers
Parent notes on legends and dated passages

units.title: Unit 1: Kings and Outlaws of Old England

lessons.title: Lesson 1: King Alfred and the Cakes and King Alfred and the Beggar
steps: Read “King Alfred and the Cakes” and “King Alfred and the Beggar” aloud together
Tell back both Alfred stories in order: the burned cakes, then the beggar at the door
Draw Alfred by the hearth with the cakes smoking
questions: Why did King Alfred let the cakes burn?
What did Alfred give the beggar?
answers: He was busy thinking about how to gather his army and beat the Danes
Half of his only loaf and half of his wine

lessons.title: Lesson 2: King Canute on the Seashore and The Sons of William the Conqueror
steps: Read “King Canute on the Seashore” and “The Sons of William the Conqueror” aloud together
Narrate how Canute taught his officers a lesson, then what each prince chose to be
Draw Canute's chair at the water's edge, or the three princes' birds

links.label: Read “The Sons of William the Conqueror”

questions: What did Canute command the sea to do?
Which bird did Henry, the Handsome Scholar, choose?
answers: Come no farther and not touch his feet
A starling

lessons.title: Lesson 3: The White Ship
steps: Read “The White Ship” aloud together
Narrate the voyage of the White Ship from the merry start to the sad end
Draw the white ship with its white sails under the full moon
questions: Why did Prince William row back to the sinking ship?
answers: To save his little sister
lessons.notes: The ending is sad: the prince and nearly everyone aboard drown. The poem at the end is a nice one to read aloud.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: King John and the Abbot
steps: Read “King John and the Abbot” aloud together
Narrate the three questions and the shepherd's three clever answers
Draw the shepherd throwing off the abbot's gown before King John
questions: What did the shepherd say the king was thinking?
answers: That he was the Abbot of Canterbury, but he was only the abbot's shepherd

lessons.title: Lesson 5: A Story of Robin Hood
steps: Read “A Story of Robin Hood” aloud together
Narrate how Robin Hood helped Allin-a-Dale
Draw Robin Hood dressed as a harper at the church door
questions: What did Robin Hood do when he blew his horn three times?
answers: He called twenty-four of his men in green, with Allin-a-Dale among them, into the church
lessons.notes: Baldwin admits Robin was a lawless outlaw; a good chance to talk about whether robbing the rich is ever right.

units.title: Unit 2: Scotland, Gotham, and Brave Englishmen

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Bruce and the Spider and The Black Douglas
steps: Read “Bruce and the Spider” and “The Black Douglas” aloud together
Narrate what Bruce learned from the spider, then how the Black Douglas took the castle
Draw the spider's web under the shed, or the men creeping like cattle toward the wall
questions: How many times did the spider try before her thread reached the beam?
What did the watchman think the Black Douglas and his men were?
answers: Seven
The farmer's cattle

lessons.title: Lesson 7: Three Men of Gotham and Other Wise Men of Gotham
steps: Read “Three Men of Gotham” and “Other Wise Men of Gotham” aloud together
Retell the quarrel on the bridge, then the silly things the sheriff saw in Gotham
Draw one of the 'foolish' things the men of Gotham were doing
questions: How did the man with the sack show Hodge and Peter they were foolish?
Why did the men of Gotham act like fools?
answers: He poured all his meal into the river, then asked how much was in the sack
So the king's sheriff would think them simple and not cut off their noses

lessons.title: Lesson 8: The Miller of the Dee and Sir Philip Sidney
steps: Read “The Miller of the Dee” and “Sir Philip Sidney” aloud together
Narrate why the miller was happy, then what Sir Philip Sidney did with the cup of water
Draw the miller at work in his mill by the river
questions: Which river turned the happy miller's mill?
Who did Sir Philip Sidney give his water to?
answers: The River Dee
A dying soldier lying nearby

lessons.title: Lesson 9: The Ungrateful Soldier and Sir Humphrey Gilbert
steps: Read “The Ungrateful Soldier” and “Sir Humphrey Gilbert” aloud together
Narrate what the Danish soldier did after the Swede shot at him, then Sir Humphrey Gilbert's last voyage
Draw the little 'Squirrel' among the icebergs
questions: How did the Dane 'punish' the Swede who shot at him?
What were the names of the two ships?
answers: He drank half the water and gave him only the other half
The Squirrel and the Golden Hind
lessons.notes: The Gilbert story describes America as roamed by 'wild Indians'; you might point out that many Native nations already had towns and farms here.

lessons.title: Lesson 10: Sir Walter Raleigh
steps: Read “Sir Walter Raleigh” aloud together
Narrate the cloak and the puddle, and the two plants Raleigh brought home
Draw Raleigh spreading his scarlet cloak over the puddle
questions: What two things from America did Raleigh make known in England?
answers: The potato and tobacco
lessons.notes: Calls the Native people 'savage Indians.' Worth a quick talk about where potatoes and tobacco came from: Native farmers had grown them for centuries.

units.title: Unit 3: Heroes of America, the Sea, and the Mountains

lessons.title: Lesson 11: Pocahontas and George Washington and his Hatchet
steps: Read “Pocahontas” and “George Washington and his Hatchet” aloud together
Narrate the Pocahontas story, then the cherry tree story
Draw young George with his hatchet
questions: What did Pocahontas do to save John Smith?
What did George's father say he would rather lose than hear one lie?
answers: She threw herself between him and the clubs and laid her head on his
A dozen cherry trees
lessons.notes: Both are legends: historians doubt Smith's rescue tale (the book itself says some tales are untrue), and the cherry tree story was invented by an early biographer. Pocahontas was about 11 at the time; the book calls the Powhatan people simply 'Indians' and their leader 'king.'

lessons.title: Lesson 12: Grace Darling
steps: Read “Grace Darling” aloud together
Narrate the rescue from the night of the storm to the lighthouse
Draw Grace and her father rowing toward the wreck
questions: Who rowed out with Grace to save the shipwrecked men?
answers: Her father, the lighthouse keeper
lessons.notes: This really happened, in 1838, off the coast of northeast England.

lessons.title: Lesson 13: The Story of William Tell and Arnold Winkelried
steps: Read “The Story of William Tell” and “Arnold Winkelried” aloud together
Narrate William Tell and the apple, then how Arnold Winkelried broke the lines
Draw Tell's arrow and the apple, or Arnold running at the spears
questions: What did Tell say the second arrow was for?
What did Arnold Winkelried cry as he ran at the spears?
answers: For the tyrant's heart, if he had hurt his child
Make way for liberty!
lessons.notes: Find Switzerland on a map. Arnold's story ends with his death for his country.

lessons.title: Lesson 14: The Bell of Atri
steps: Read “The Bell of Atri” aloud together
Narrate the story of the bell of justice and the old horse
Draw the starving horse pulling on the grapevine rope
questions: What did the judges order the miser to do?
answers: Set aside half his gold to give the horse food, a pasture and a warm stall

lessons.title: Lesson 15: How Napoleon crossed the Alps and The Story of Cincinnatus
steps: Read “How Napoleon crossed the Alps” and “The Story of Cincinnatus” aloud together
Narrate Napoleon's march over the Alps, then how Cincinnatus saved Rome
Draw Cincinnatus leaving his plow in the field
questions: What word did Napoleon say a man who means to win never uses?
How many days was Cincinnatus ruler of Rome?
answers: Impossible
Sixteen
lessons.notes: The Cincinnatus story calls Rome's enemies 'half-wild' and 'savage' men; that is the Romans' side of the story.

lessons.title: Lesson 16: The Story of Regulus and Cornelia's Jewels
steps: Read “The Story of Regulus” and “Cornelia's Jewels” aloud together
Narrate why Regulus went back to Carthage, then what Cornelia called her jewels
Draw Cornelia with her two sons beside her
questions: Why did Regulus go back to prison in Carthage?
What did Cornelia say were her jewels?
answers: Because he had promised to, and a Roman keeps his word
Her two sons
lessons.notes: Regulus goes back to a cruel death; the story stays brief about it.

lessons.title: Lesson 17: Androclus and the Lion
steps: Read “Androclus and the Lion” aloud together
Narrate the story of Androclus and the lion
Draw Androclus pulling the thorn from the lion's paw
questions: What was hurting the lion?
answers: A long, sharp thorn in his paw
lessons.notes: Androclus was enslaved, and the crowd came to watch him be killed. A gentle opening to talk about slavery in Rome.

lessons.title: Lesson 18: Horatius at the Bridge
steps: Read “Horatius at the Bridge” aloud together
Narrate how Horatius kept the bridge
Draw Horatius on the bridge, or leaping into the Tiber
questions: Which river did Horatius swim across?
answers: The Tiber

lessons.title: Lesson 19: Julius Cæsar and The Sword of Damocles
steps: Read “Julius Cæsar” and “The Sword of Damocles” aloud together
Narrate the two Caesar stories, then what Damocles saw over his head
Draw Damocles at the feast with the sword hanging above
questions: What did Caesar say he would rather be than the second man in Rome?
What held up the sword over Damocles?
answers: The head man of a village
A single horsehair

units.title: Unit 5: Stories of Greece (and a Hawk)

lessons.title: Lesson 20: Damon and Pythias and A Laconic Answer
steps: Read “Damon and Pythias” and “A Laconic Answer” aloud together
Narrate how Damon trusted his friend, then the Spartans' one-word answer
Draw Pythias arriving at the prison door just in time
questions: Why was Pythias late coming back?
What one word did the Spartans send back to King Philip?
answers: He was delayed by storms and shipwreck
If
lessons.notes: Try being 'laconic' at lunch: answer in as few words as you can.

lessons.title: Lesson 21: The Ungrateful Guest and Alexander and Bucephalus
steps: Read “The Ungrateful Guest” and “Alexander and Bucephalus” aloud together
Narrate the ungrateful guest, then how Alexander tamed Bucephalus
Draw young Alexander turning Bucephalus toward the sun
questions: How had the farmer helped the soldier?
What was Bucephalus afraid of?
answers: He cared for him after he was washed up half-drowned from a shipwreck
His own shadow

lessons.title: Lesson 22: Diogenes the Wise Man and The Brave Three Hundred
steps: Read “Diogenes the Wise Man” and “The Brave Three Hundred” aloud together
Narrate the two Diogenes stories, then the stand of the three hundred
Draw Diogenes by his tub, or Diogenes with his lantern
questions: What did Diogenes ask Alexander to do for him?
Who led the three hundred Spartans in the pass?
answers: Stand aside so he would not block the sunshine
Leonidas, King of the Spartans
lessons.notes: Leonidas's men all die in battle; you can keep the telling short for little ones.

lessons.title: Lesson 23: Socrates and his House and The King and his Hawk
steps: Read “Socrates and his House” and “The King and his Hawk” aloud together
Narrate Socrates's small house, then the story of the king and his hawk
Draw the hawk swooping at the silver cup
questions: What did Socrates hope to fill his little house with?
Why did the hawk keep knocking the cup away?
answers: True friends
A poisonous dead snake was lying in the spring
lessons.notes: Genghis Khan kills his hawk before he understands; the lesson is never to act in anger.

lessons.title: Lesson 24: Doctor Goldsmith and The Kingdoms
steps: Read “Doctor Goldsmith” and “The Kingdoms” aloud together
Narrate Doctor Goldsmith's 'medicine,' then the king's three questions to the children
Draw the children around the king in the meadow
questions: What was really in Goldsmith's box of 'medicine'?
To what kingdom did the boy say the orange belonged?
answers: Money
The vegetable kingdom

lessons.title: Lesson 25: The Barmecide Feast
steps: Read “The Barmecide Feast” aloud together
Narrate the pretend feast and the real one
Draw the Barmecide and Schacabac at the empty table
questions: Why did the Barmecide invite Schacabac to live with him?
answers: Because he was good-humored and quick-witted and made the best of everything

lessons.title: Lesson 26: The Endless Tale and The Blind Men and the Elephant
steps: Read “The Endless Tale” and “The Blind Men and the Elephant” aloud together
Narrate the locust story the stranger told, then what each blind man thought
Draw the six blind men around the elephant

links.label: Read “The Blind Men and the Elephant”

questions: What did the locusts keep carrying away?
What did the man who held the tail say the elephant was like?
answers: Grains of corn, one at a time
A rope

lessons.title: Lesson 27: Maximilian and the Goose Boy
steps: Read “Maximilian and the Goose Boy” aloud together
Narrate the king, the book, and the geese
Draw the king chasing the geese with the whip
questions: What did the goose boy say the king would never be?
answers: A good gooseherd

lessons.title: Lesson 28: The Inchcape Rock
steps: Read “The Inchcape Rock” aloud together
Narrate what the Abbot did and what Ralph the Rover did
Draw the bell on the buoy above the rock
questions: What did Ralph the Rover do to the bell?
answers: He cut it loose so it sank into the sea

lessons.title: Lesson 29: Whittington and his Cat (Parts I–II)
steps: Read parts I–II of “Whittington and his Cat” aloud together
Narrate how Dick came to London and why he bought a cat
Draw the eight-horse wagon on the road to London
questions: What did Dick hear people say London's streets were paved with?
Why did Dick buy a cat?
answers: Gold
To drive away the rats and mice in his garret
lessons.notes: Read parts I and II (The City, The Kitchen) today.

lessons.title: Lesson 30: Whittington and his Cat (Parts III–V)
steps: Read parts III–V of “Whittington and his Cat” aloud together
Narrate the ship's voyage, the cat at the palace, and Dick's fortune
Draw the cat chasing the rats from the king's table
questions: What did the bells of Bow Church seem to say to Dick?
Whom did Dick marry?
answers: Turn again, Whittington, thrice Lord Mayor of London
Alice, Mr. Fitzwarren's daughter
lessons.notes: Read parts III–V (The Venture, The Cat, The Fortune). The book says the people there had 'never seen any white men' and pokes fun at the queen's English; a good chance to talk about how travelers' tales treated other peoples.

lessons.title: Lesson 31: Casabianca
steps: Read “Casabianca” aloud together
Narrate what happened on the burning ship
Draw the boy standing on the deck
questions: Why would Casabianca not leave the ship?
answers: His father had told him to stay at his post, and he did not know his father was dead
lessons.notes: This is a sad story of war (the Battle of the Nile, 1798). Read ahead if you have a sensitive child.

lessons.title: Lesson 32: Antonio Canova
steps: Read “Antonio Canova” aloud together
Narrate how Antonio saved the Count's dinner
Draw the butter lion on the Count's table
questions: What did Antonio carve his lion from?
answers: A big lump of butter

lessons.title: Lesson 33: Picciola
steps: Read “Picciola” aloud together
Narrate how Charney cared for his little plant
Draw Picciola growing between the paving stones
questions: Who helped Charney save the plant and get set free?
answers: The emperor's wife (Napoleon's empress), after reading his handkerchief

lessons.title: Lesson 34: Mignon
steps: Read “Mignon” aloud together
Narrate how Mignon came to live with Wilhelm and how she tried to please him
Draw Mignon dancing blindfolded among the eggs
questions: What did Mignon dance among without touching any?
answers: Eggs laid out on a carpet
lessons.notes: From Goethe's novel. Mignon tries to scrub the brown tint off her skin, thinking it is dye; you may want to talk about that. The story ends without a real ending.
